newsitem.title: UK: Time running out for ferry fire safety changes.
newsitem.headline: Time running out for ferry fire safety changes.

text.p: Ferry and passengership operators who have not yet taken action to implement new fire safety regulations are running out of time, Lloyd's Register warned on Thursday.
Senior surveyor for the British classification society's construction services department, Allan Barrett, said: "The timescale left is very short."
"For those who have not thought about the 1992 SOLAS amendments, it is fast becoming an impossibility to comply with the regulations" he said.
Several of the safety of life at sea (SOLAS) amendments to fire regulations which were adopted in 1992 become applicable from October 1, 1997.

They include the fitting of smoke detectors and alarm systems, fire doors, low level lighting in passenger areas and the use of non-combustible furniture in stairway enclosures. Pre-1974 built vessels will also require sprinkler systems.

From October 1, 2000, all stairways in accommodation and service spaces will need to be of steel frame construction and some ventilation ducts will have to be fitted with fail-safe automatic closing fire dampers. These could involve major modifications, he said.
Barrett said Lloyd's Register was authorised to inspect 87 ro-ro vessels and 12 cruiseships for application of the amendments.

"We have visited about 60, made reports to the owners and made various callbacks to look at individual installations. To date we have only one existing vessel which fully complies with the amendments."
He added that the U.S. Coast Guard had warned owners not to sail to the U.S. if they had not implemented all the amendments as it took the attitude they had had plenty of time to put them in place.
However, Barrett admitted that the feasibility of some of the amendments was still questionable.

"Cold stores are an area Lloyd's Register is having difficulties in coming to grips with," he said, accepting complaints that conditions inside freezer rooms would falsely set off fire alarms and that sprinklers were useless within them.

Barrett said Lloyd's Register had expressed its misgivings to other members of the International Association of Classification Societies (IACS) and that attempts were being made to overcome the problems at sub-committees of the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).
